Free Printable Hive Inspection Sheet (PDF) — Beekeeping Record

This is a free, one-page printable hive inspection sheet in PDF format. Each row is one inspection of one hive: date and conditions, whether you saw the queen or eggs, what the brood pattern looked like, honey and pollen stores, temperament, pests and varroa count, and what you did and plan to do next visit. Inspections are the heart of beekeeping records — the thing you notice at a hive is only useful if you can compare it with the last visit — and a one-line row per inspection is the format most beekeepers settle on. Blank columns are deliberate: a sheet that is fast to fill in at the hive gets filled in.

When and how often to inspect

During the active season most beekeepers open a hive every 7 to 10 days — often enough to catch swarm preparations, which take about that long from egg to capped queen cell, and seldom enough not to set the colony back. Inspect on a warm, calm, sunny day when foragers are out and the hive is calmer and emptier. In cold months, inspections are brief or skipped; heft the hive to judge stores instead and log that.

Keep the sheet short at the hive and add detail afterwards if needed. Eggs seen means the queen was present within the last three days even if you never saw her; that one tick replaces a long search. Write the varroa count from an alcohol wash or sugar roll as mites per 100 bees so visits are comparable — the varroa mite calculator on this site does the arithmetic.

What to check and what it usually means

CheckLooks rightWorth noting
Queen / eggsEggs standing upright in cells: queen laid within ~3 daysNo eggs or young larvae for two visits; multiple eggs per cell (laying workers)
Brood patternSolid, compact capped brood with few empty cellsSpotty pattern, sunken or perforated cappings, discolored larvae
Queen cellsNone, or a few play cupsCharged swarm cells along frame bottoms; supersedure cells on the face
StoresBand of pollen and honey around the brood; frames of capped honeyLight hive going into dearth or winter; no pollen
SpaceBees covering most frames with room to expandBearding and congestion (add space); too much empty space in a weak hive
TemperamentCalm bees, little followingSudden defensiveness: queenless, dearth, robbing, or weather
Pests / diseaseFew hive beetles, no wax moth webbing, mite count lowRising mite count; deformed wings; beetles in numbers; foul smell

Thresholds and treatment choices vary by region and season — use your local association's guidance. The sheet records what you saw; it does not prescribe treatment.

How to use this sheet

  1. Print the PDF — one sheet per hive, or one shared sheet for a small apiary — and keep it in the toolbox or on a clipboard.
  2. Before opening, write the date, weather, and what you intend to check; after, fill the row while it is fresh.
  3. Tick Queen or Eggs; note the brood pattern in a word or two (solid, spotty); estimate stores in frames.
  4. Record mite counts as mites per 100 bees from a wash or roll, and any pests seen.
  5. Finish with what you did (added a super, swapped frames) and what the next visit should check.

Questions

Is this sheet really free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print — no sign-up, no email, no watermark.

How often should I inspect a beehive?

Roughly every 7 to 10 days during the active season, less often in cool weather and rarely in winter. The interval matters for swarm control — a capped queen cell can appear within about eight days of the egg being laid.

Do I need to find the queen every time?

No. Eggs are proof the queen was laying within the last three days. Most experienced beekeepers look for eggs and young larvae and only search for the queen when they need to mark, move, or replace her.

How do I record a varroa count?

As mites per 100 bees from an alcohol wash or sugar roll — a half cup of bees is about 300, so divide the mites found by three. The varroa mite calculator on this site does the conversion.
